title: Kontomire Stew with Plantain
author: Afua Boateng
desc: Cocoyam leaves with goat, crab and smoked fish — and the cue that matters is the agushi beginning to clump in the sauce after a few minutes.
longDesc: Kontomire stew is the other half of ampesi and it is one of the great dishes of the Akan kitchen. A cup of palm oil softens the onions; blended tomatoes and pepper go in and simmer until they start to fry, three to five minutes; then marinated goat, smoked fish and crabs. The kontomire follows, and then the soaked agushi — ground melon seeds — stirred in very gently. The cue is exact and worth knowing: the agushi begins to clump in the sauce after a few minutes. Ten to fifteen minutes on low and it is done. Turkey berries and calabash nutmeg are in the list.
ingredients: 1 lb kontomire (cocoyam) leaves, washed and chopped — spinach works
2 lb goat meat — chicken or beef acceptable
2 medium onions and a handful of shallots
steps: Soften the onions in the palm oil.
Add the blended tomatoes and pepper and leave to simmer until it starts to fry, stirring about 3 to 5 minutes.
Add the marinated goat, the smoked fish and the crabs.
Add the soaked agushi while stirring very gently, and leave to simmer — the agushi begins to clump in the sauce after a few minutes.
Leave to simmer on low heat about 10 to 15 minutes.
Meanwhile boil the plantains about 15 minutes, and serve alongside.
chefTips: The agushi clumping is the cue and it is the whole character of the dish — you want soft lumps of melon seed suspended in the sauce, not a smooth thickened gravy.
Stir very gently once the agushi is in. Vigorous stirring breaks the clumps up and you lose the texture entirely.
Until it starts to fry is the tomato cue — the moment the water has cooked off and the oil comes back out. Three to five minutes of stirring.
A cup of palm oil is a lot and it is correct. Kontomire stew is a rich dish and the oil carries the leaf.
Turkey berries, alligator pepper and calabash nutmeg are all in the list and all are genuinely Ghanaian — the turkey berries are bitter little green globes and they are not a garnish.
Crabs boiled five minutes separately, then added. They are in for flavour as much as for eating.
Grate the calabash nutmeg fresh. One to two whole nutmegs is a strong aromatic hit and it is one of the markers of a properly made kontomire stew.
commonMistakes: Stirring hard after the agushi goes in, destroying the clumps.
Adding the tomatoes and moving on before they start to fry.
Substituting true nutmeg for calabash nutmeg.
Cooking the leaves so long they lose their colour.
sources: Adapted from 'Recipe: Kontomire Stew With Plantain', modernghana.com, Thursday 2 November 2017. BYLINE FLAG: the byline prints as 'By Mywekutastes.com', which is a site's own name, not a person.

Ingredients exactly as printed: 2 Pounds goat meat (chicken or beef acceptable); 2 Large crabs; 1 Smoked fish; 1 Pound washed chopped Kontomire leaves or taro (spinach works); 1/2 cup ground Agushi (melon seeds); 1 Cup Palm oil; 2 Medium onions and handful of shallots; 1 Blended onion; Handful of Turkey berries; 7-10 Medium tomatoes; 1/4 Teaspoon cayenne pepper; 1-2 Garlic cloves; Dash of alligator pepper; 1-2 Grated calabash nutmegs; 1-2 Scotch bonnet peppers; 5 Fingers of plantain; Salt to taste.

Method as printed: boil the crabs about 5 minutes; soften the onions in palm oil; add the blended tomatoes and pepper and 'Leave to simmer until it starts to fry. Stir it for about 3-5 minutes', then add the marinated goat, 'smoked salmon' and crabs; add the kontomire; 'Add the soaked agushi whilst stirring very gently and leave to simmer. The agushi begins to clump in the sauce after a few minutes.'; 'Leave to simmer on low heat for about 10-15 minutes'; boil plantains about 15 minutes.

INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY, flagged and NOT corrected: the ingredient list says 'Smoked fish' and the method says 'smoked salmon'. These are different things and the source does not reconcile them. The ingredient list's wording is used above.

THE AGUSHI CUE, verbatim, and the best technique note in the kontomire record: 'The agushi begins to clump in the sauce after a few minutes.' Together with 'stirring very gently', it tells you the texture you are aiming for.
THE TOMATO CUE, verbatim: 'Leave to simmer until it starts to fry.'

A SECOND VERSION, from a named Ghanaian author, with two different bylines for one recipe: Afia Amoako, 'Vegan Kontomire/Palava Stew'. On eatwithafia.com the byline reads 'Written by support', published 16 November 2020, updated 20 January 2026, yield 5 servings. On thecanadianafrican.com the same recipe is bylined 'By Afia' with yield 'Serves 4'. The two sites appear to belong to the same person, and ONE RECIPE CARRIES TWO BYLINES AND TWO YIELDS — recorded as an unreconciled discrepancy. Its ingredients: 2 small onions (1 finely chopped, 1 roughly chopped); 2-3 garlic cloves; 1/3 scotch bonnet or habanero; 1 thumb-size ginger; 2 tomatoes; 2 tbsp tomato paste; 2 tbsp palm oil; 1 tsp curry powder; ½ tsp each garlic and onion powder; ½ tsp anise seeds; ½ tsp coriander seeds; 2 tsp veggie bouillon; 1 cup whole egusi; ½ block firm tofu; ⅔ cup water; salt; 1 packet frozen spinach, thawed. ITS METHOD CONTAINS A MISPRINT OR EXTRACTION LOSS — 'fry for minutes' with the number missing — which has NOT been filled in. Its cues are useful and are quoted: the tofu goes in when 'the oil starts to separate'; the egusi dollops cook 6-10 minutes covered; greens go in at low heat, with '20+ minutes for cocoyam leaves'. That last figure is the only published cooking time for cocoyam leaves found anywhere. It is a VEGAN ADAPTATION with an egusi-and-tofu base and is not a traditional Akan preparation.

A BRANDED VERSION, recorded not published: the Tasty Tom Cookbook (Olam Group), 'Kontomire Abom Sauce', pages 2-3, serves 4-5, no date or individual author, built on 4 tablespoons of its own tomato product with 2 bunches kontonmire, 1 large koobi, 2 eggs, 1 avocado, kpakpo shito, ginger and 2 cooking spoons of oil. Its method roasts the onions and tomatoes on charcoal and grinds them in a clay pot — a genuinely traditional technique — but it is a corporate brand cookbook and not a neutral source.

A FOURTH SOURCE, ingredients only: Fafa Gilbert, 'How to make the tastiest Kontomire Stew (Cocoyam leaves)', 13 April 2021 — method is video-only. FLAG: Gilbert is Ewe rather than Akan, and her list includes '500g grilled salmon' alongside 450g pre-cooked cocoyam leaves, 500g smoked mackerel, 2 tins tuna, 40g dried anchovies (Abobi), 300g melon seeds with 200ml water, 3 banana shallots, 30ml zomi, 70g baby plum tomatoes, 1 habanero, 20g ginger, 4-5 mild green chillies, 1 tbsp all-purpose spice and 1 tsp chilli flakes.
For the palaver sauce question — whether kontomire stew and palaver sauce are the same dish — see GHA024.
reheating: Gentle heat. Do not stir hard or the agushi clumps break down.
healthBenefits: Cocoyam leaves are exceptionally high in vitamin A, vitamin C, iron and calcium.
Melon seeds supply plant protein, magnesium and zinc.
Red palm oil contributes provitamin-A carotenoids and tocotrienols.
Crab and smoked fish both add lean protein, iodine and selenium.
culturalNote: Kontomire stew with ampesi is the everyday Akan plate, and the clumps of agushi suspended in dark green leaf and red oil are what it should look like. Turkey berries, alligator pepper and calabash nutmeg in one ingredient list is a good sign that a recipe was written by someone cooking it rather than describing it.
